concepts.name: Origin and Transformation of the Maratha Confederacy
key_dimensions: Transition from centralized Maratha kingdom under Shivaji to a confederacy under the Peshwas
Role of the Battle of Khed (1707) and Balaji Vishwanath in institutionalizing the confederacy
Distinction between the nominal sovereignty of Chhatrapati and the de facto power of the Peshwa
UPSC trap: Confusing the confederacy's formation timeline with Shivaji's original administrative system

concepts.name: The Peshwas: Rise, Powers, and Administrative Role
key_dimensions: Evolution of Peshwa from a ministerial post to the de facto head of the confederacy
Key Peshwas — Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) — and their distinct contributions
Peshwa's relationship with the Chhatrapati: constitutional subordination vs. practical dominance
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which Peshwa expanded territory vs. who consolidated administration vs. who presided over decline

concepts.name: The Five Chief Houses of the Maratha Confederacy
key_dimensions: The five principal chiefs: Peshwas (Pune), Bhonsles (Nagpur), Scindias/Shindes (Gwalior), Holkars (Indore), Gaekwads (Baroda)
Territorial jurisdiction, military strength, and political loyalties of each house
Inter-house rivalries and their exploitation by the British East India Company
UPSC trap: Confusing the geographic domains of Scindias vs. Holkars vs. Bhonsles, and mixing up their roles in the Anglo-Maratha Wars

concepts.name: Baji Rao I and the Expansion of the Confederacy
key_dimensions: Military campaigns: Gujarat, Malwa, Bundelkhand, and the raid on Delhi (1737)
Strategic vision of a 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' (Hindu political supremacy) — its meaning and limitations
Relationships with Mughal governors and the nature of Maratha suzerainty vs. direct administration
UPSC trap: Overattributing the concept of Hindu Pad Padshahi as a formal policy vs. a rhetorical aspiration

concepts.name: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi: Revenue and Political Instruments
key_dimensions: Definition, rates (1/4 and 1/10 of revenue), and legal basis of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi
Distinction between the two levies: Chauth as protection tax vs. Sardeshmukhi as a hereditary claim
Geographic extent of collection and its role in financing confederacy expansion
UPSC trap: Confusing which levy was collected by whom (Peshwa vs. Chhatrapati vs. individual chiefs) and conflating them with regular land revenue

concepts.name: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761): Causes, Course, and Consequences
key_dimensions: Immediate causes: Afghan invasion of Ahmad Shah Durrani, Maratha overextension into northern India
Role of internal confederacy divisions — Holkars' non-participation, absence of Nizam's support
Short-term vs. long-term consequences: military setback vs. eventual Maratha recovery under Madhavrao I
UPSC trap: Attributing the defeat solely to military factors while ignoring diplomatic failures and logistical overstretch

concepts.name: Madhavrao I (Peshwa): Revival of the Confederacy Post-Panipat
key_dimensions: Administrative and fiscal reforms to rebuild Maratha power after 1761
Military reassertion in northern India: restoration of Maratha influence at Delhi
Managing internal confederacy conflicts including Raghunathrao's (Raghoba's) ambitions
UPSC trap: Underrating Madhavrao I's significance relative to Baji Rao I — both are high-yield but for different reasons

concepts.name: The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782) and the Treaty of Salbai
key_dimensions: British intervention in the Peshwa succession dispute (Raghoba/Raghunathrao controversy)
Convention of Wadgaon (1779): British defeat and its political significance
Treaty of Salbai (1782): terms, territorial status quo, and its role in giving the British time to consolidate
UPSC trap: Confusing the Treaty of Purandar (1776) with the Treaty of Salbai, and misattributing who gained what

concepts.name: The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–1805) and the Subsidiary Alliance
key_dimensions: Treaty of Bassein (1802): Peshwa Baji Rao II's acceptance of British Subsidiary Alliance and its implications
Military campaigns: Arthur Wellesley's victories at Assaye and Argaon against Scindias and Bhonsles
Treaties of Deogaon (Bhonsle) and Surji-Anjangaon (Scindia): territorial losses
UPSC trap: Conflating the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha Wars, and misidentifying which chief signed which treaty

concepts.name: The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–1818) and the Dissolution of the Confederacy
key_dimensions: Triggering events: Peshwa Baji Rao II's attack on the British Residency at Pune (Kirkee)
Simultaneous British campaigns against Peshwa, Bhonsle (Nagpur), and Holkar (Indore)
Consequences: Abolition of the Peshwaship, annexation of Peshwa territories, pensioning of Baji Rao II at Bithur
UPSC trap: The Gaekwad of Baroda did NOT actively oppose the British in this war — understanding why some chiefs survived

concepts.name: Subsidiary Alliance System and the Maratha Confederacy
key_dimensions: Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance: terms, obligations, and strategic purpose against the confederacy
Differential application: which Maratha chiefs accepted (Peshwa, Bhonsle, Scindia, Holkar) and when
How the alliance structurally dismantled Maratha military independence before open conflict
UPSC trap: The Holkars were the last to accept the Subsidiary Alliance (1818) — not all chiefs accepted simultaneously

concepts.name: Internal Conflicts and Fragmentation within the Confederacy
key_dimensions: Holkar vs. Scindia rivalry: Battle of Ujjain (1728) origins and recurring conflicts
Peshwa succession disputes: Narayan Rao's assassination, Raghoba controversy, and British exploitation
Lack of a unified command structure: how confederacy design inherently limited collective military response
UPSC trap: Framing all internal conflicts as the 'reason for decline' — need to balance with British strategic superiority

concepts.name: Maratha Administrative System under the Confederacy
key_dimensions: Dual administrative layers: Peshwa's central administration vs. autonomous administration of chief houses
Revenue system: continuity and modification of Shivaji's original system under confederacy chiefs
Role of Amatya, Sachiv, and other Ashta Pradhan positions under the confederacy vs. their original design
UPSC trap: Assuming the Ashta Pradhan (Eight Ministers) functioned as effectively under the confederacy as under Shivaji

concepts.name: Maratha Military System and Innovations under the Confederacy
key_dimensions: Evolution from guerrilla warfare (Shivaji's model) to conventional warfare under confederacy chiefs
Role of European military commanders: De Boigne and Perron for Scindias; influence on artillery and infantry
Financial basis of military power: Chauth revenue, plunder, and its unsustainability
UPSC trap: Overemphasizing European-trained infantry as the decisive factor while ignoring supply chain and political failures

concepts.name: The Bhonsles of Nagpur: Role and Significance in the Confederacy
key_dimensions: Raghuji Bhonsle I's expansion into Bengal, Orissa, and Central India — distinct from other confederacy chiefs
Bhonsles' semi-independent posture within the confederacy and periodic conflicts with Peshwas
Treaty of Deogaon (1803) and eventual integration into the British system
UPSC trap: Confusing Nagpur Bhonsles with the original Bhonsle clan of Shivaji (Satara branch) — two distinct lines

concepts.name: Mahadaji Scindia: Reassertion of Maratha Power and Diplomacy
key_dimensions: Mahadaji's role in rehabilitating Maratha prestige after Panipat and the First Anglo-Maratha War
Control of the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II: Maratha protectorate over Delhi and its political symbolism
Treaty negotiations and balancing British, Mughal, and Rajput interests
UPSC trap: Attributing the zenith of Scindia power to later rulers — Mahadaji (d. 1794) was the peak, not Daulat Rao Scindia

concepts.name: Nana Fadnavis: Diplomacy, Administration, and the Confederacy's Last Coherence
key_dimensions: Role as de facto administrator during weak Peshwa rule (Sawai Madhavrao period)
Diplomatic maneuvering against British expansion and inter-confederacy rivalries
Impact of his death (1800) on the cohesion of confederacy resistance to the British
UPSC trap: Conflating Nana Fadnavis's diplomatic legacy with military power — he was primarily a statesman, not a military commander

concepts.name: Maratha Confederacy and the Rajput/Jat/Sikh States: Alliances and Conflicts
key_dimensions: Nature of Maratha overlordship over Rajput states: tribute-extraction vs. genuine alliance
Maratha-Jat relations: conflict and cooperation around Delhi and the Doab region
Why Marathas failed to forge a sustained anti-British Hindu coalition with Rajputs and Sikhs
UPSC trap: Assuming Maratha relations with northern Indian powers were uniformly antagonistic — there were tactical alliances

concepts.name: The Treaty of Bassein (1802): Turning Point in Anglo-Maratha Relations
key_dimensions: Context: Peshwa Baji Rao II's defeat by Holkar at Hadapsar and his flight to British protection
Terms of Bassein: Subsidiary Alliance acceptance, territorial concessions, and loss of sovereign foreign policy
Reaction of other confederacy chiefs (Scindias, Bhonsles) and why it triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War
UPSC trap: Treating Bassein as a bilateral agreement — it fundamentally altered the entire confederacy's relationship with the British

concepts.name: Decline of the Maratha Confederacy: Multi-Causal Analysis
key_dimensions: Structural weaknesses: decentralized confederacy design, inter-chief rivalries, absence of a unified command
British advantages: superior diplomacy (Subsidiary Alliance), financial resources, and divide-and-rule strategy
Socio-economic factors: unsustainable revenue model (Chauth), overextension, and failure to modernize governance
UPSC trap: Single-cause explanations (e.g., 'Panipat caused the decline') — the UPSC rewards multi-dimensional analysis
